topic.title: Food: The community fridge on Elm Street
topic.focus: The community fridge on Elm Street

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-10. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: A simple idea
sections.text: Two years ago, a group of neighbours in a small English town put an old fridge in a wooden shed on Elm Street. The idea was simple: anyone can leave food they do not need, and anyone can take food for free. The fridge is open every day from eight in the morning until eight in the evening. A sign on the door says, "Take what you need, leave what you can."

sections.heading: Who uses it
sections.text: At first, people thought only poor families would use the fridge. In fact, all kinds of people visit it. Students take bread and vegetables at the end of the week. Older people bring extra fruit from their gardens in summer. A local baker leaves unsold cakes every evening, and they are usually gone within an hour.

sections.heading: Keeping it safe
sections.text: Volunteers check the fridge twice a day. They clean the shelves, look at the dates on the food, and throw away anything that is too old. Fresh meat and fish are not allowed because they can become dangerous quickly. There is a book inside the shed where visitors can write what they took, but writing in it is not required.

sections.heading: Problems along the way
sections.text: The project has had some difficulties. One winter, the fridge broke and the group had no money to fix it. A local shop heard about the problem and paid for a new fridge the next week. Sometimes people leave open packets or home-cooked meals, which the volunteers must remove for safety reasons.

sections.heading: More than food
sections.text: The organisers say the fridge has done more than reduce food waste. Neighbours who never spoke before now stop and talk by the shed. A retired teacher gives free English lessons to new families she met at the fridge. The group hopes to open a second fridge near the train station next year.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — A simple idea
Two years ago, a group of neighbours in a small English town put an old fridge in a wooden shed on Elm Street. The idea was simple: anyone can leave food they do not need, and anyone can take food for free. The fridge is open every day from eight in the morning until eight in the evening. A sign on the door says, "Take what you need, leave what you can."

Paragraph 2 — Who uses it
At first, people thought only poor families would use the fridge. In fact, all kinds of people visit it. Students take bread and vegetables at the end of the week. Older people bring extra fruit from their gardens in summer. A local baker leaves unsold cakes every evening, and they are usually gone within an hour.

Paragraph 3 — Keeping it safe
Volunteers check the fridge twice a day. They clean the shelves, look at the dates on the food, and throw away anything that is too old. Fresh meat and fish are not allowed because they can become dangerous quickly. There is a book inside the shed where visitors can write what they took, but writing in it is not required.

Paragraph 4 — Problems along the way
The project has had some difficulties. One winter, the fridge broke and the group had no money to fix it. A local shop heard about the problem and paid for a new fridge the next week. Sometimes people leave open packets or home-cooked meals, which the volunteers must remove for safety reasons.

Paragraph 5 — More than food
The organisers say the fridge has done more than reduce food waste. Neighbours who never spoke before now stop and talk by the shed. A retired teacher gives free English lessons to new families she met at the fridge. The group hopes to open a second fridge near the train station next year.
